claims.text: Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings is primarily governed by interfaces between distinct alloy layers.
The interfaces create heterogeneous microstructural barriers.
The interfacial barriers pin and impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion retards creep deformation under sustained loads.
A controlled comparison can use an engineered multilayer coating and a monolithic coating having the same overall alloy composition.
Thermally activated dislocation motion is expected under the proposed high-temperature, constant-stress conditions.
Interface coherency, misfit strain, and interface density determine the effectiveness of interfaces as dislocation-pinning sites.
Multilayer interfaces obstruct dislocation glide.
Multilayer interfaces obstruct dislocation climb.
Compositional gradients and stress fields introduced by the interfaces cause their obstacle effect.
The increased density of barriers reduces steady-state creep rate relative to a homogeneous single-phase material.
The multilayer coating will have a significantly lower creep rate than the monolithic baseline.
The multilayer coating will undergo less microstructural evolution than the monolithic baseline.
The multilayer coating will contain fewer mobile dislocations than the monolithic baseline after creep exposure.
The monolithic coating is expected to creep faster because it lacks engineered interface barriers.
The proposed behavior applies in temperature and stress regimes where thermally activated dislocation motion controls deformation.
Interfacial pinning may become ineffective when layer thickness lies outside an optimal range.
Activation of additional deformation mechanisms may alter the predicted behavior.
Interface-induced barrier effects are well established in other multilayer systems.
The relative contributions of high-entropy compositional complexity and multilayer interfaces have not been fully quantified for these coatings.
